```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Live Google Sheet (switch back to this once the module is running):
# df = pd.read_csv("https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/e/2PACX-1vRWIOZ03GpUJgqvGVmI9cih169mMq0ajLMj6a0VTd2tytB3K5BmX5AUiKQ8FKIL6KUKEcgb-1LR-1eM/pub?gid=0&single=true&output=csv")
# Synthetic data for building/testing slides before the module runs:
df = pd.read_csv("data/synthetic_reaction_times.csv")

# Normalise column name — sheet uses 'name', dummy data uses 'student_name'
if 'name' in df.columns and 'student_name' not in df.columns:
    df = df.rename(columns={'name': 'student_name'})

# Handle caffeine column — may not exist in early data
if 'caffeine' not in df.columns:
    df['caffeine'] = 'Unknown'
df['caffeine'] = df['caffeine'].fillna('Unknown')

students = sorted(df["student_name"].unique().tolist())

# Per-student summary (one row per student for frequency tables)
students_df = df.drop_duplicates('student_name')

device_freq = (
    students_df.groupby('device').size()
    .reset_index(name='count')
)
device_freq['pct'] = (device_freq['count'] / device_freq['count'].sum() * 100).round(1)

caff_freq = (
    students_df.groupby('caffeine').size()
    .reset_index(name='count')
)
caff_freq['pct'] = (caff_freq['count'] / caff_freq['count'].sum() * 100).round(1)

student_stats = (
    df.groupby(["student_name", "device", "caffeine"])["reaction_time_ms"]
    .agg(mean="mean", median="median", sd="std", min="min", max="max")
    .reset_index()
    .round(1)
)

# NaN (e.g. missing finger_mm on older submissions) is not valid JSON. All
# ojs_define() values share one JSON payload, so a single stray NaN anywhere
# breaks every variable in the call — clean before handing over.
df_clean = df.astype(object).where(df.notna(), None)
student_stats_clean = student_stats.astype(object).where(student_stats.notna(), None)

ojs_define(
    data         = df_clean.to_dict(orient="records"),
    students     = students,
    pool_mean    = round(float(df["reaction_time_ms"].mean()), 1),
    pool_med     = round(float(df["reaction_time_ms"].median()), 1),
    pool_sd      = round(float(df["reaction_time_ms"].std()), 1),
    pool_max     = int(df["reaction_time_ms"].max()),
    pool_min     = int(df["reaction_time_ms"].min()),
    smry         = student_stats_clean.to_dict(orient="records"),
    device_freq  = device_freq.to_dict(orient="records"),
    caff_freq    = caff_freq.to_dict(orient="records"),
)
```

## {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {style="text-align: center; padding-top: 180px;"}
[**How do we understand a variable?**]{style="font-size: 2.2em; color: white;"}

[Before any model, any test, any result — you need to know what your data actually looks like.]{style="font-size: 1.1em; color: #aaa; padding-top: 20px; display: block;"}
:::

## What is exploratory data analysis?

::: {.instructions-box}
**Exploratory data analysis (EDA)** is the process of describing your variables — the values they take, how often they take them, and whether anything is unusual. 

This is the **crucial** step to take before you do anything else with the data.
:::

Békés & Kézdi frame it as three questions to ask before any model:

- How should you start the analysis itself?
- How do you describe the data and present its key features?
- How do you explore the data and check whether it's clean enough for further analysis?

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:24px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), *Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy*, Ch. 3
:::

## Why bother with EDA?

Five reasons:

1. **To check data cleaning** — EDA is part of an iterative cleaning process
2. **To guide subsequent analysis** — what you see shapes what you do next
3. **To give context** for interpreting later results
4. **To ask additional questions** — EDA can refine the research question itself
5. It can **offer simple, but possibly important, answers** on its own

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:24px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3
:::

## The business question

::: {.instructions-box}
A regional bank's customer service centre measures agent **response time** — how quickly an agent reacts to an incoming alert. It's a key operational metric.

HR currently records **one test score per agent**, taken once at onboarding, and uses it to rank and place staff.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Is a single measurement an adequate way to capture this metric?**

That's the question we'll answer today — using data we collect ourselves.
:::

## Collect the data

::: {.instructions-box}
1. Open **stevenolanecon.github.io/7002LBSAI/week1-tool.html** on your phone or laptop
2. Enter your name, select your device, answer the caffeine question, and measure your **index finger length** with a ruler (tip to base crease, mm)
3. Complete **10 trials** — tap as soon as the screen turns green
4. Your results save automatically when you finish
:::

Results go directly to the class dataset. We will explore them together today and in the coming weeks.

## Tidy data

Every row is one **observation**. Every column is one **variable**.

```{ojs}
html`<table style="width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.88em;margin-top:16px;">
  <thead>
    <tr style="background:#1a1a2e;color:white;">
      <th style="padding:10px 18px;text-align:left;">student_name</th>
      <th style="padding:10px 18px;text-align:left;">trial</th>
      <th style="padding:10px 18px;text-align:left;">reaction_time_ms</th>
      <th style="padding:10px 18px;text-align:left;">device</th>
      <th style="padding:10px 18px;text-align:left;">caffeine</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    ${data.slice(0,5).map((r,i) => `
      <tr style="${i%2===1?'background:#fafafa;':''}border-bottom:1px solid #eee;">
        <td style="padding:9px 18px;">${r.student_name}</td>
        <td style="padding:9px 18px;text-align:center;">${r.trial}</td>
        <td style="padding:9px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;color:#457b9d;">${r.reaction_time_ms}</td>
        <td style="padding:9px 18px;">${r.device}</td>
        <td style="padding:9px 18px;">${r.caffeine || '—'}</td>
      </tr>`).join('')}
    <tr><td colspan="5" style="padding:9px 18px;color:#888;font-style:italic;font-size:0.9em;">… ${data.length} rows total (10 trials × ${students.length} students)</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>`
```

::: {.fragment}
This format makes filtering, grouping, and plotting straightforward.
One student's data = filter by `student_name`. One trial type = filter by `trial`. One device group = filter by `device`.
:::

# Section C {background-color="#2d6a4f"}
## Visualising distributions

---

## Frequency, probability, distribution

- **Absolute frequency** — the count of observations with a particular value
- **Relative frequency** — that count expressed as a proportion, or percentage, of all observations
- **Probability** generalises relative frequency: a measure of the likelihood of an event, always between 0 and 1 — and, unlike relative frequency, it can describe an event without needing a dataset at all
- The **distribution** of a variable tells you the frequency of each value it takes in the data, independent of what the other variables show

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:20px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3
:::

## Visualisation

- Statistics are useful but it often (always?) useful to **look** at your data
- There are many ways to understanding the distribution of your variables
- Histograms are the most famous 

## What is a histogram?

A histogram is a bar chart of a variable's distribution — bars show how many observations (or what percentage) fall in each bin.

Reading one, look for:

| Feature | What to look for |
|---|---|
| **Modes** | Peaks that stand out from their neighbourhood |
| **Centre and tails** | Where most of the mass sits, and how it thins out |
| **Symmetry** | Symmetric, or a long left/right tail? |
| **Extreme values** | Points far from the rest, out in the tails |

::: {.fragment}
Now let's build one from data we collected ten minutes ago.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3
:::

      Plot.dot(student_data_trials,  { x: "trial", y: "reaction_time_ms", fill: "#457b9d", r: 9,

## Pooled histogram

```{ojs}
viewof hist_controls = {
  const f = html`<div style="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:24px;flex-wrap:wrap;
                              font-size:13px;font-family:'Helvetica Neue',sans-serif;
                              padding:6px 2px;color:#333;">
    <label style="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:8px;">
      <span style="color:#666;white-space:nowrap;">Bin width</span>
      <input type="range" name="bin_width" min="10" max="80" step="10" value="30"
             style="width:100px;cursor:pointer;accent-color:#457b9d;">
      <span id="bw-label" style="font-weight:600;min-width:34px;color:#457b9d;">30 ms</span>
    </label>
    <label style="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:8px;">
      <span style="color:#e63946;white-space:nowrap;font-weight:600;">Exclude above</span>
      <input type="range" name="threshold" min="${pool_min}" max="${Math.ceil(pool_max/10)*10 + 10}" step="10" value="${Math.ceil(pool_max/10)*10 + 10}"
             style="width:110px;cursor:pointer;accent-color:#e63946;">
      <span id="thr-label" style="font-weight:600;min-width:40px;color:#e63946;">All</span>
    </label>
    <label style="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:6px;cursor:pointer;">
      <input type="checkbox" name="show_mean" checked style="cursor:pointer;accent-color:#e63946;"> Mean
    </label>
    <label style="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:6px;cursor:pointer;">
      <input type="checkbox" name="show_median" style="cursor:pointer;accent-color:#f4a261;"> Median
    </label>
    <label style="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:6px;cursor:pointer;">
      <input type="checkbox" name="show_kde" style="cursor:pointer;accent-color:#2d6a4f;"> KDE
    </label>
    <label style="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:6px;cursor:pointer;">
      <input type="checkbox" name="show_pct" style="cursor:pointer;accent-color:#333;"> Show as %
    </label>
  </div>`

  const bwRange  = f.querySelector('[name=bin_width]')
  const bwLabel  = f.querySelector('#bw-label')
  const thrRange = f.querySelector('[name=threshold]')
  const thrLabel = f.querySelector('#thr-label')

  bwRange.addEventListener('input', () => {
    bwLabel.textContent = bwRange.value + ' ms'
    f.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('input'))
  })
  const thrMax = Math.ceil(pool_max / 10) * 10 + 10
  thrRange.addEventListener('input', () => {
    thrLabel.textContent = +thrRange.value >= thrMax ? 'All' : thrRange.value + ' ms'
    f.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('input'))
  })
  f.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]').forEach(cb =>
    cb.addEventListener('change', () => f.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('input')))
  )
  Object.defineProperty(f, 'value', { get() { return {
    bin_width:  +f.querySelector('[name=bin_width]').value,
    threshold:  +f.querySelector('[name=threshold]').value,
    show_mean:   f.querySelector('[name=show_mean]').checked,
    show_median: f.querySelector('[name=show_median]').checked,
    show_kde:    f.querySelector('[name=show_kde]').checked,
    show_pct:    f.querySelector('[name=show_pct]').checked,
  }}})
  return f
}
```

```{ojs}
{
  const thr      = hist_controls.threshold
  const thrMax   = Math.ceil(pool_max / 10) * 10 + 10
  const filtered = data.filter(d => d.reaction_time_ms <= thr)
  const vals     = filtered.map(d => d.reaction_time_ms)
  const mu       = d3.mean(vals)
  const med      = d3.median(vals)
  const sigma    = d3.deviation(vals)
  const excluded = data.length - filtered.length
  const bw       = hist_controls.bin_width
  const pct      = hist_controls.show_pct

  const pad  = Math.max(20, Math.round((d3.max(vals) - d3.min(vals)) * 0.1))
  const xmin = Math.floor((d3.min(vals) - pad) / 10) * 10
  const xmax = Math.ceil((thr + pad) / 10) * 10

  // KDE — Epanechnikov kernel, Silverman's bandwidth
  // Absolute mode scales density to expected count per bin; relative mode
  // scales it to the same proportion-per-bin units as the "proportion" reducer.
  const h = sigma * 1.06 * Math.pow(vals.length, -0.2)
  const kdePoints = d3.range(xmin, xmax, 2).map(x => {
    const density = d3.mean(vals, v => {
      const u = (x - v) / h
      return Math.abs(u) <= 1 ? 0.75 * (1 - u * u) / h : 0
    })
    return { x, y: pct ? density * bw : density * filtered.length * bw }
  })

  return Plot.plot({
    height: 330,
    marginLeft: 55,
    marginBottom: 32,
    x: { label: "Reaction time (ms)", domain: [xmin, xmax] },
    y: pct
      ? { label: "% of trials", percent: true }
      : { label: "Count" },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(filtered,
        Plot.binX({ y: pct ? "proportion" : "count" },
          { x: "reaction_time_ms", thresholds: d3.range(xmin, xmax + bw, bw),
            fill: "#457b9d", fillOpacity: 0.75 })),
      Plot.ruleX([0]),
      hist_controls.show_mean   ? Plot.ruleX([mu],  { stroke: "#e63946", strokeWidth: 2.5,
                             strokeDasharray: "6,4",
                             tip: true, title: () => `Mean: ${mu.toFixed(1)} ms` }) : null,
      hist_controls.show_median ? Plot.ruleX([med], { stroke: "#f4a261", strokeWidth: 2.5,
                             strokeDasharray: "6,4",
                             tip: true, title: () => `Median: ${med.toFixed(1)} ms` }) : null,
      hist_controls.show_kde    ? Plot.line(kdePoints, { x: "x", y: "y",
                             stroke: "#2d6a4f", strokeWidth: 2.5 }) : null,
      excluded > 0 ? Plot.text([{ x: xmax, y: 0 }], {
                             text: () => `${excluded} value${excluded > 1 ? 's' : ''} excluded`,
                             x: "x", frameAnchor: "top-right",
                             fill: "#e63946", fontSize: 12, fontStyle: "italic" }) : null,
    ]
  })
}
```

::: {.fragment}
Wider bins can smooth away real structure and suggest a more gradual decline than the data actually shows — bin width is a choice, not a neutral default.
:::

## Shape and outliers

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
**What the histogram tells us**

| Feature | What we see |
|---------|-------------|
| **Floor** | ~150 ms minimum |
| **Tail** | Long tail to the right |
| **Skew** | Right-skewed |
| **KDE** | Smoothed shape of the distribution |

:::
::: {.col .fragment}
**Outliers**

There is some theoretical minimum - no human can react instantaneously. 

There is no ceiling. Distraction, hesitation, accidental clicks — all extend the right tail.


:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Task** — In Excel: experiment with bin width. Try plotting reaction times split by device and by caffeine group.
:::

## What do we do with an outlier?

For every extreme value, ask three questions — in order:

| Question | If yes | Reaction-time example |
|---|---|---|
| **Is it an error?** | Drop or fix it | A 4 ms trial — a mis-click before the screen turned green |
| **Is it real, but not what we're studying?** | Drop it, with a note | A slow trial because the student was talking to a neighbour |
| **Is it a genuine feature of the process?** | Keep it | A slow trial from real hesitation — this *is* operational variability |

::: {.fragment}
The decision changes what you're measuring. Dropping every slow trial doesn't just clean the data — it can quietly redefine the metric.
:::

---

# Section D {background-color="#2d6a4f"}
## Summary statistics

---

## What is a summary statistic?

For any variable, a **statistic** is a meaningful number you can compute from the data. **Summary statistics** describe the most important features of a distribution — its centre, its spread, its shape.

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:20px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3
:::

## The mean and expected value

It is standard to refer to our variable as $x$. The mean (or average) of $x$ is calculated as: 

$$\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}$$
If we have $a$ and $b$ that are fixed whilst $x$ varies we get two useful properties: $\overline{x+a} = \bar{x} + a$ and $\overline{x \cdot b} = \bar{x} \cdot b$.

::: {.fragment}
The **expected value**, $E[x]$, is the value you'd expect for a randomly chosen observation.

- For a quantitative variable, $E[x]$ is the mean
- For a binary variable coded 0/1 — like *caffeine* — $E[x]$ is the **probability**, or relative frequency, of the category coded 1
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3
:::

## Median, quantiles, mode

- **Median** — the middle value when sorted; half the observations lie below, half above
- **Quantiles / percentiles** divide the data into proportions. **Quartiles** divide it into fourths — the median is the 2nd quartile, the 50th percentile
- **Mode** — the most frequent value; some distributions have more than one

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:20px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3
:::

## Centre: mean vs median

```{ojs}
viewof centre_student = Inputs.select(students, {
  label: null,
  value: students[2]
})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const sd   = data.filter(d => d.student_name === centre_student)
  const vals = sd.map(d => d.reaction_time_ms).sort((a,b) => a - b)
  const mu   = d3.mean(vals)
  const med  = d3.median(vals)
  const cPad = Math.max(30, Math.round((d3.max(vals) - d3.min(vals)) * 0.2))
  const cMin = d3.min(vals) - cPad
  const cMax = d3.max(vals) + cPad
  const jittered = vals.map(v => ({ v, y: (Math.random() - 0.5) * 0.8 }))

  return Plot.plot({
    height: 240,
    marginLeft: 55,
    x: { label: "Reaction time (ms)", domain: [cMin, cMax] },
    y: { axis: null, domain: [-1, 1] },
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(jittered, { x: "v", y: "y", fill: "#457b9d", r: 5, fillOpacity: 0.65 }),
      Plot.ruleX([mu],  { stroke: "#e63946", strokeWidth: 3,
                          tip: true, title: () => `Mean: ${mu.toFixed(1)} ms` }),
      Plot.ruleX([med], { stroke: "#f4a261", strokeWidth: 3,
                          tip: true, title: () => `Median: ${med.toFixed(1)} ms` }),
      Plot.text([{ x: mu,  label: `Mean\n${mu.toFixed(1)}`  }],
                { x: "x", text: "label", dy: -28, fill: "#e63946", fontSize: 13 }),
      Plot.text([{ x: med, label: `Median\n${med.toFixed(1)}` }],
                { x: "x", text: "label", dy: 38,  fill: "#f4a261", fontSize: 13 }),
    ]
  })
}
```

::: {.fragment}
**Mean** — sum ÷ *n*. The balance point. Sensitive to every value, including outliers.

**Median** — the middle value when sorted. Robust to extreme values.

**Mode** — the most frequent value. Most useful for discrete or categorical data.

When mean and median diverge, ask *why*. The answer is usually the shape of the distribution.
:::

::: {.fragment}
After the workshop, go back to the histogram and drag the "exclude above" threshold down. Watch how much the **mean** moves compared to the **median** as the slowest trials drop out — that gap *is* the sensitivity to outliers.
:::

## Variance and standard deviation

$$Var[x] = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n} \qquad SD[x] = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n}}$$

- **Variance** is the average *squared* deviation from the mean — harder to interpret directly, but easy to work with algebraically because it is itself a mean
- **Standard deviation** is the square root of variance — back in the original units, and roughly the typical distance between a randomly chosen observation and the mean

::: {.fragment}
Two distributions can share a mean but differ in spread: the higher the SD, the more dispersed the data. In finance, SD is literally how volatility is measured — a higher SD means a price that jumps around more.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3
:::

## Spread: SD and IQR

```{ojs}
viewof spread_student = Inputs.select(students, {
  label: null,
  value: students[4]
})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const sd   = data.filter(d => d.student_name === spread_student)
  const vals = sd.map(d => d.reaction_time_ms)
  const mu   = d3.mean(vals)
  const sig  = d3.deviation(vals)
  const q1   = d3.quantile(vals.slice().sort((a,b) => a-b), 0.25)
  const q3   = d3.quantile(vals.slice().sort((a,b) => a-b), 0.75)

  const sPad = Math.max(30, Math.round((d3.max(vals) - d3.min(vals)) * 0.2))
  const sMin = d3.min(vals) - sPad
  const sMax = d3.max(vals) + sPad
  const jittered = vals.map(v => ({ v, y: (Math.random() - 0.5) * 1.0 }))

  return Plot.plot({
    height: 220,
    marginLeft: 55,
    x: { label: "Reaction time (ms)", domain: [sMin, sMax] },
    y: { axis: null },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectX([{ x1: q1, x2: q3 }],
        { x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: -0.6, y2: 0.6, fill: "#f4a261", fillOpacity: 0.25 }),
      Plot.rectX([{ x1: mu - sig, x2: mu + sig }],
        { x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: -0.6, y2: 0.6, fill: "#e63946", fillOpacity: 0.15 }),
      Plot.dot(jittered, { x: "v", y: "y", fill: "#457b9d", r: 5, fillOpacity: 0.7 }),
      Plot.ruleX([mu], { stroke: "#e63946", strokeWidth: 2.5 }),
      Plot.text([
        { x: mu,        label: `Mean: ${mu.toFixed(1)}`          },
        { x: mu - sig,  label: `−1 SD (${(mu-sig).toFixed(0)})` },
        { x: mu + sig,  label: `+1 SD (${(mu+sig).toFixed(0)})` },
      ], { x: "x", text: "label", dy: -32, fill: "#e63946", fontSize: 11 }),
      Plot.text([
        { x: (q1+q3)/2, label: `IQR: ${q1.toFixed(0)}–${q3.toFixed(0)} ms` }
      ], { x: "x", text: "label", dy: 38, fill: "#f4a261", fontSize: 12 }),
    ]
  })
}
```

::: {.fragment}
**Range** = max − min. Simple but dominated by extremes.

**SD** = √variance. Same units as the data. Sensitive to outliers.

**IQR** = Q3 − Q1. Spread of the middle 50%. Robust to outliers.

**90–10 range** = 90th percentile − 10th percentile. A middle ground — trims the most extreme 20% without being as narrow as the IQR.
:::

## Standardised values and skewness

Standardising expresses a value in units of standard deviation:

$$x_{\text{standardised}} = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{SD[x]}$$

A standardised value of 1 means "one SD above the mean"; −1 means "one SD below."

::: {.fragment}
A distribution is **skewed** if it isn't symmetric. A simple measure:

$$\text{Skewness} = \frac{\bar{x} - \text{median}(x)}{SD[x]}$$

When the right tail is long, the mean sits above the median and skewness is positive — exactly why our reaction-time data is right-skewed.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3
:::

## Box plot and violin plot: our data

```{ojs}
{
  const allVals = data.map(d => d.reaction_time_ms)
  const bPad = Math.max(30, Math.round((d3.max(allVals) - d3.min(allVals)) * 0.1))
  const bMin = Math.floor((d3.min(allVals) - bPad) / 10) * 10
  const bMax = Math.ceil((d3.max(allVals) + bPad) / 10) * 10
  const colours = { Phone: "#457b9d", Laptop: "#2d6a4f" }

  const grouped = ["Phone", "Laptop"].map(dev => {
    const vals = data.filter(d => d.device === dev).map(d => d.reaction_time_ms).sort((a,b) => a-b)
    const q1 = d3.quantile(vals,0.25), q3 = d3.quantile(vals,0.75)
    const iqr = q3 - q1
    const fenceLo = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, fenceHi = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    const inRange = vals.filter(v => v >= fenceLo && v <= fenceHi)
    return {
      group: dev,
      q1, q2: d3.quantile(vals,0.5), q3,
      lo: d3.min(inRange), hi: d3.max(inRange), mean: d3.mean(vals),
    }
  })

  const fenceLookup = Object.fromEntries(grouped.map(g => [g.group, g]))
  const outliers = data.filter(d => {
    const g = fenceLookup[d.device]
    return d.reaction_time_ms < g.lo || d.reaction_time_ms > g.hi
  })

  return Plot.plot({
    height: 190,
    marginLeft: 80,
    x: { label: "Reaction time (ms)", domain: [bMin, bMax] },
    y: { label: null, type: "band" },
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(data,      { x: "reaction_time_ms", y: "device",
                            fill: d => colours[d.device], r: 4, fillOpacity: 0.2, jitter: "y" }),
      Plot.ruleY(grouped, { y: "group", x1: "lo", x2: "hi", stroke: d => colours[d.group], strokeWidth: 1.5 }),
      Plot.barX(grouped,  { x1: "q1", x2: "q3", y: "group", insetTop: 14, insetBottom: 14,
                            fill: d => colours[d.group], fillOpacity: 0.55,
                            stroke: d => colours[d.group], strokeWidth: 2 }),
      Plot.tickX(grouped, { x: "q2", y: "group", insetTop: 14, insetBottom: 14, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 3 }),
      Plot.dot(grouped,   { x: "mean", y: "group", fill: d => colours[d.group], stroke: "white",
                            strokeWidth: 1, r: 6, symbol: "diamond" }),
      Plot.dot(outliers,  { x: "reaction_time_ms", y: "device",
                            stroke: d => colours[d.device], fill: "white", r: 5, strokeWidth: 1.5 }),
    ]
  })
}
```

```{ojs}
{
  const groups = ["Phone", "Laptop"]
  const yPos = { Phone: 1, Laptop: 0 }
  const colours = { Phone: "#457b9d", Laptop: "#2d6a4f" }
  const allVals = data.map(d => d.reaction_time_ms)
  const bPad = Math.max(30, Math.round((d3.max(allVals) - d3.min(allVals)) * 0.1))
  const bMin = Math.floor((d3.min(allVals) - bPad) / 10) * 10
  const bMax = Math.ceil((d3.max(allVals) + bPad) / 10) * 10

  const violinData = groups.flatMap(g => {
    const vals = data.filter(d => d.device === g).map(d => d.reaction_time_ms)
    if (vals.length < 2) return []
    const sigma = d3.deviation(vals)
    const h = sigma * 1.06 * Math.pow(vals.length, -0.2)
    const xs = d3.range(bMin, bMax, 2)
    const dens = x => d3.mean(vals, v => {
      const u = (x - v) / h
      return Math.abs(u) <= 1 ? 0.75 * (1 - u * u) / h : 0
    })
    const maxDensity = d3.max(xs, dens)
    return xs.map(x => {
      const norm = maxDensity ? (dens(x) / maxDensity) * 0.42 : 0
      return { group: g, x, y1: yPos[g] - norm, y2: yPos[g] + norm }
    })
  })

  return Plot.plot({
    height: 190,
    marginLeft: 80,
    x: { label: "Reaction time (ms)", domain: [bMin, bMax] },
    y: { domain: [-0.7, 1.7], ticks: [0, 1],
         tickFormat: v => v === 1 ? "Phone" : v === 0 ? "Laptop" : "", label: null },
    marks: groups.map(g => Plot.areaY(violinData.filter(d => d.group === g),
      { x: "x", y1: "y1", y2: "y2", fill: colours[g], fillOpacity: 0.5, stroke: colours[g], strokeWidth: 1.5 })),
  })
}
```

::: {.fragment}
Box = IQR · Line = median · Diamond = mean · Whiskers = furthest point within 1.5×IQR of the box · Open circles = outliers beyond that. Violin = the same distribution, shown as its full shape rather than five summary numbers.
:::

## Python does this for you

Ultimatly, in your working life you will not be calculting all these statistics yourself. Rather, you'll use statistical software. Here is what the Python output looks like: 

```python
import statsmodels.stats.descriptivestats as smd
print(smd.describe(df["reaction_time_ms"]))
```

```{python}
#| output: asis
import statsmodels.stats.descriptivestats as smd

_desc = smd.describe(df["reaction_time_ms"])["reaction_time_ms"]
_rows = [
    ("nobs", f"{_desc['nobs']:.0f}"),
    ("mean", f"{_desc['mean']:.1f}"),
    ("std_err", f"{_desc['std_err']:.1f}"),
    ("upper_ci", f"{_desc['upper_ci']:.1f}"),
    ("lower_ci", f"{_desc['lower_ci']:.1f}"),
    ("std", f"{_desc['std']:.1f}"),
    ("iqr", f"{_desc['iqr']:.1f}"),
    ("skewness", f"{_desc['skew']:.2f}"),
    ("kurtosis", f"{_desc['kurtosis']:.2f}"),
    ("mode", f"{_desc['mode']:.1f}"),
    ("median", f"{_desc['median']:.1f}"),
]
_line_width = 16
_lines = "<br>".join(k + "&nbsp;" * (_line_width - len(k)) + v for k, v in _rows)

print(
    '::: {style="font-family: monospace; font-size: 0.78em; background: #f8f8f8; '
    'border-left: 4px solid #457b9d; padding: 14px 20px; border-radius: 4px; line-height: 1.9;"}\n'
    f'{_lines}\n:::'
)
```

:::

## So — was a single test score enough?

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
Go back to HR's onboarding test: **one trial, one number, one ranking.**

Every student here just produced **10** trials — and for most, the spread between fastest and slowest trial was far bigger than the difference between students.
:::
::: {.col .fragment}
A single measurement doesn't tell you someone's typical response time. It tells you where **one random draw** from their distribution happened to land.

**HR's test is measuring noise as if it were signal.**
:::
:::

```{ojs}
{
  const allVals = data.map(d => d.reaction_time_ms)
  const bPad = Math.max(30, Math.round((d3.max(allVals) - d3.min(allVals)) * 0.1))
  const bMin = Math.floor((d3.min(allVals) - bPad) / 10) * 10
  const bMax = Math.ceil((d3.max(allVals) + bPad) / 10) * 10
  const colours = { Phone: "#457b9d", Laptop: "#2d6a4f" }

  const grouped = ["Phone", "Laptop"].map(dev => {
    const vals = data.filter(d => d.device === dev).map(d => d.reaction_time_ms).sort((a,b) => a-b)
    const q1 = d3.quantile(vals,0.25), q3 = d3.quantile(vals,0.75)
    const iqr = q3 - q1
    const fenceLo = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, fenceHi = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    const inRange = vals.filter(v => v >= fenceLo && v <= fenceHi)
    return { group: dev, q1, q2: d3.quantile(vals,0.5), q3,
             lo: d3.min(inRange), hi: d3.max(inRange), mean: d3.mean(vals) }
  })

  const fenceLookup = Object.fromEntries(grouped.map(g => [g.group, g]))
  const outliers = data.filter(d => {
    const g = fenceLookup[d.device]
    return d.reaction_time_ms < g.lo || d.reaction_time_ms > g.hi
  })

  return Plot.plot({
    height: 280,
    marginLeft: 80,
    x: { label: "Reaction time (ms)", domain: [bMin, bMax] },
    y: { label: null, type: "band" },
    marks: [
      show_pts_device
        ? Plot.dot(data, { x: "reaction_time_ms", y: "device",
                           fill: d => colours[d.device], r: 4, fillOpacity: 0.2, jitter: "y" })
        : null,
      Plot.ruleY(grouped, { y: "group", x1: "lo", x2: "hi", stroke: d => colours[d.group], strokeWidth: 1.5 }),
      Plot.barX(grouped,  { x1: "q1", x2: "q3", y: "group", insetTop: 22, insetBottom: 22,
                            fill: d => colours[d.group], fillOpacity: 0.55,
                            stroke: d => colours[d.group], strokeWidth: 2 }),
      Plot.tickX(grouped, { x: "q2", y: "group", insetTop: 22, insetBottom: 22, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 3 }),
      Plot.dot(grouped,   { x: "mean", y: "group", fill: d => colours[d.group], stroke: "white",
                            strokeWidth: 1, r: 6, symbol: "diamond" }),
      Plot.dot(outliers, { x: "reaction_time_ms", y: "device",
                           stroke: d => colours[d.device], fill: "white", r: 5, strokeWidth: 1.5 }),
    ]
  })
}
```

## Does caffeine matter?

```{ojs}
viewof show_pts_caff = Inputs.toggle({ label: "Show individual points", value: true })
```

```{ojs}
{
  const colours = { Yes: "#e63946", No: "#457b9d" }
  const allVals = data.map(d => d.reaction_time_ms)
  const bPad = Math.max(30, Math.round((d3.max(allVals) - d3.min(allVals)) * 0.1))
  const bMin = Math.floor((d3.min(allVals) - bPad) / 10) * 10
  const bMax = Math.ceil((d3.max(allVals) + bPad) / 10) * 10

  const grouped = ["Yes", "No"].map(c => {
    const vals = data.filter(d => d.caffeine === c).map(d => d.reaction_time_ms).sort((a,b) => a-b)
    if (!vals.length) return null
    const q1 = d3.quantile(vals,0.25), q3 = d3.quantile(vals,0.75)
    const iqr = q3 - q1
    const fenceLo = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, fenceHi = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    const inRange = vals.filter(v => v >= fenceLo && v <= fenceHi)
    return { group: c, q1, q2: d3.quantile(vals,0.5), q3,
             lo: d3.min(inRange), hi: d3.max(inRange), mean: d3.mean(vals) }
  }).filter(Boolean)

  const pointData = data.filter(d => d.caffeine === "Yes" || d.caffeine === "No")

  const fenceLookup = Object.fromEntries(grouped.map(g => [g.group, g]))
  const outliers = pointData.filter(d => {
    const g = fenceLookup[d.caffeine]
    return g && (d.reaction_time_ms < g.lo || d.reaction_time_ms > g.hi)
  })

  return Plot.plot({
    height: 280,
    marginLeft: 80,
    x: { label: "Reaction time (ms)", domain: [bMin, bMax] },
    y: { label: "Caffeine?", type: "band" },
    marks: [
      show_pts_caff
        ? Plot.dot(pointData, { x: "reaction_time_ms", y: "caffeine",
                                fill: d => colours[d.caffeine], r: 4, fillOpacity: 0.2, jitter: "y" })
        : null,
      Plot.ruleY(grouped, { y: "group", x1: "lo", x2: "hi", stroke: d => colours[d.group], strokeWidth: 1.5 }),
      Plot.barX(grouped,  { x1: "q1", x2: "q3", y: "group", insetTop: 22, insetBottom: 22,
                            fill: d => colours[d.group], fillOpacity: 0.55,
                            stroke: d => colours[d.group], strokeWidth: 2 }),
      Plot.tickX(grouped, { x: "q2", y: "group", insetTop: 22, insetBottom: 22, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 3 }),
      Plot.dot(grouped,   { x: "mean", y: "group", fill: d => colours[d.group], stroke: "white",
                            strokeWidth: 1, r: 6, symbol: "diamond" }),
      Plot.dot(outliers, { x: "reaction_time_ms", y: "caffeine",
                           stroke: d => colours[d.caffeine], fill: "white", r: 5, strokeWidth: 1.5 }),
    ]
  })
}
```

## Comparing groups: the numbers

```{ojs}
{
  function summarise(vals) {
    if (!vals.length) return { n: 0, mean: "—", median: "—", min: "—", max: "—", sd: "—", skew: "—" }
    const sorted = vals.slice().sort((a,b) => a-b)
    const mu  = d3.mean(sorted)
    const med = d3.median(sorted)
    const sig = d3.deviation(sorted)
    return {
      n: sorted.length,
      mean: mu.toFixed(1),
      median: med.toFixed(1),
      min: d3.min(sorted),
      max: d3.max(sorted),
      sd: sig !== undefined ? sig.toFixed(1) : "—",
      skew: sig ? ((mu - med) / sig).toFixed(2) : "—",
    }
  }

  const rows = [
    { group: "Phone",  ...summarise(data.filter(d => d.device === "Phone").map(d => d.reaction_time_ms)) },
    { group: "Laptop", ...summarise(data.filter(d => d.device === "Laptop").map(d => d.reaction_time_ms)) },
  ]

  return html`<table style="width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.95em;margin-top:16px;">
    <thead>
      <tr style="background:#1a1a2e;color:white;">
        <th style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:left;">Device</th>
        <th style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">N</th>
        <th style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">Mean</th>
        <th style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">Median</th>
        <th style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">Min</th>
        <th style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">Max</th>
        <th style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">SD</th>
        <th style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">Skew</th>
      </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
      ${rows.map((r,i) => `
        <tr style="${i%2===1?'background:#fafafa;':''}border-bottom:1px solid #eee;">
          <td style="padding:10px 16px;font-weight:600;">${r.group}</td>
          <td style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">${r.n}</td>
          <td style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">${r.mean}</td>
          <td style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">${r.median}</td>
          <td style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">${r.min}</td>
          <td style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">${r.max}</td>
          <td style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">${r.sd}</td>
          <td style="padding:10px 16px;text-align:right;">${r.skew}</td>
        </tr>`).join('')}
    </tbody>
  </table>`
}
```

::: {.fragment}
A chart plus a table is the standard way to present a group comparison — the chart shows shape, the table gives exact numbers to quote.
:::



## Can we claim a difference is real?

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
**We can see differences in the charts.**

But is the class the *population* we care about?

- If **yes** — we have all the data. No inference needed. The difference is the difference.
- If **no** — we are treating the class as a **sample** from a larger group (all students? all adults?).

:::
::: {.col .fragment}
**This is the inference question.**

Any sample will show differences between groups — **by chance alone**.

*How do we decide which differences to take seriously?*

That requires thinking about **sampling**, **variability**, and **probability**.

**That's Week 2.**
:::
:::

## Six steps of EDA

1. Start with the variables that matter most
2. Qualitative variables — list frequencies
3. Quantitative variables — look at the histogram
4. Check for extreme values. Decide what to do with them, deliberately
5. Look at summary statistics — let them guide further questions
6. Explore further if needed — by group, over time, or otherwise

::: {.fragment}
Every one of these steps, we just did.
:::
